# Interview Tips & Notes

These are **practical study notes**, separate from the book-based interview lessons that will be created after you upload source material. The aim is not to memorise impressive phrases. It is to demonstrate that you understand a problem and can explain how you reached a decision.

## Start with three essential techniques

1. [**Structure an answer**](structuring-answers.qmd) — give the question, principle, example, limitation and conclusion in a sensible order.
2. [**Explain a system-design trade-off**](system-design-tradeoffs.qmd) — compare alternatives using a measurable objective instead of general claims.
3. [**Handle unknowns and follow-ups**](handling-follow-ups.qmd) — make assumptions explicit, reason aloud, and revise when a constraint changes.

## Mathematical techniques for solving algorithms

[**Algorithm Mathematical Techniques — 30 worked rules**](algorithm-math/index.qmd) is a dedicated third-level topic inside Tips & Notes. It collects the compact mathematics you can memorise to reconstruct algorithms: DFS invariants, recursive choice equations, prefix-sum cancellation, binary-search monotonicity, greedy exchanges, DP recurrences, number theory, and graph reasoning.

For daily recall, use the [**30-technique memory sheet**](algorithm-math/memory-sheet.qmd). Each complete lesson explains notation, substitutes actual values, proves the method and names the assumptions under which it fails.

## How to practise

Choose a topic you already know, such as Java memory ordering, a sliding-window invariant, or fair task scheduling. Explain it in **30 seconds**, then **two minutes**. Finally, answer one follow-up that changes an assumption.

Record only the aspects that were difficult: missing definitions, unsupported claims, inaccurate numbers or unclear transitions. Add corrections to your notes rather than memorising an entire script.

The tips here are original general interview guidance, not extracted from a book you have not yet supplied.
